extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and early-career researchers in mathematics (and mathematicians considering career/research choices)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for doing mathematical research and making career decisions, emphasizing adaptability in research direction, project planning, and grant writing. Focused guidance for early-career mathematicians on when to commit to problems, choose institutions, and design realistic proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared for research to be unpredictable / be flexible
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical research is by its nature unpredictable – if we knew in advance what the answer would be and how to do it, it wouldn’t be research! You should therefore be prepared for research to lead you in unexpected directions, and it may end up that you may find a new problem or area of mathematics more interesting than the one you were initially working in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect to be led to unexpected directions; be willing to switch problems or areas if they become more interesting or productive. See also linked advice to learn outside your field and to adopt other mathematicians' tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep long-term goals but update them; don't set them in stone
rubrics_metrics.description: While it is certainly worthwhile to have long-term goals, they should not be set in stone, and should be updated when new developments occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat long-term goals as living plans that evolve with new information, results, or shifts in interest. Avoid rigid commitments that prevent adaptation to better opportunities or changing circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not base career decisions purely on a single faculty member
rubrics_metrics.description: One should not base a career decision (such as what university to study at or work in) purely based on a single faculty member, since it may turn out that this faculty member may move, or that your interests change, while you are there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing institutions, evaluate multiple factors (research groups, department strength, location, mentors beyond one person) rather than tying your choice to one individual's presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid basing career choices on glamour or fame
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t base career decisions on glamour or fame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize substantive factors (research fit, training, mentorship, long-term prospects) over perceived prestige or celebrity when making career moves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't announce work on a famous problem before having a feasible plan
rubrics_metrics.description: It is generally not a good idea to announce that you are working on a well-known problem before you have a feasible plan for solving it, as this can make it harder to gracefully abandon the problem and refocus your attention in more productive directions in the event that the problem is more difficult than anticipated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid premature public commitments to big problems; they can create sunk-cost mentalities and social pressures that impede pivoting. Have feasible plans or milestones before publicizing such aims. See also 'Don't prematurely obsess on a single big problem or big theory.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Design grant proposals realistically with coherent plans and milestones
rubrics_metrics.description: In grant proposals, saying things like 'I would like to solve <Famous Problem X>' or 'I want to develop or use <Famous Theory Y>' does not impress grant reviewers unless there is a coherent plan (e.g. some easier unsolved problems to use as milestones) as well as a proven track record of progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing proposals, state achievable intermediate goals and milestones, explain methods and steps, and demonstrate a track record of relevant progress. Avoid grand, unsupported claims about solving famous problems without concrete plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be willing to abandon a problem and refocus if it proves too difficult
rubrics_metrics.description: One should be prepared to gracefully abandon a problem and refocus attention in more productive directions in the event that the problem is more difficult than anticipated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor progress realistically; if progress stalls and no feasible path appears, shift to more tractable projects or related problems that build momentum and produce publishable results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be open to learning outside your field and using other mathematicians' tools
rubrics_metrics.description: See also 'Don’t be afraid to learn things outside your field' and 'Learn the power of other mathematician’s tools.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively acquire techniques from other areas when they can illuminate your problems; cross-disciplinary learning can open new directions and methods.
